title: Trump cuts fuel economy standards back to 2014 levels
gist: The US Department of Transportation finalized a CAFE rule cutting the fuel economy target to 34.9 mpg by model year 2031, eliminating emissions credits from MY2028 and excluding plug-in vehicles from fleet averages, which may lead some automakers to drop EVs and PHEVs. The rule does tighten the light-truck loophole from MY2030, flipping the fleet mix toward passenger cars.

insights.claim: The Department of Transportation's new CAFE rule sets a target of just 34.9 mpg by model year 2031, below even the 2020 standards set during Trump's first term.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Lower efficiency mandates reduce compliance costs for automakers selling large gas vehicles.
insights.quote: The new goal is just 34.9 mpg by model year 2031.
insights.locator: The federal government’s war on fuel efficiency

insights.claim: From model year 2028 the new CAFE rule eliminates emissions credits, and plug-in vehicles will no longer count in an automaker's fleet average, whereas previously an EV or PHEV could carry a CAFE rating of hundreds of mpg.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Removes a regulatory incentive and credit-sale revenue stream that has supported EV makers.
insights.locator: Now, we may have the possibility

insights.claim: The CAFE changes raise the possibility that some automakers will drop their EVs and PHEVs entirely.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: US EV adoption and suppliers of EV components could see weaker demand.
insights.quote: Now, we may have the possibility of some OEMs dropping their EVs and PHEVs entirely.
insights.locator: Now, we may have the possibility

insights.claim: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's department told automakers in July last year it would not fine any of them for exceeding CAFE limits, going back to 2022.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Non-enforcement already removed financial penalties for high-emission fleets.

insights.claim: Separate, weaker CAFE standards for light trucks encouraged automakers to redesign crossovers as light trucks, filling roads with bigger, thirstier SUVs.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Explains the US shift toward SUVs that shaped automaker product and margin mix.

insights.claim: Starting in model year 2030, the rule changes classification criteria to flip the fleet mix from roughly 70% light trucks and 30% passenger cars to around 70% passenger cars and 30% light trucks.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Reclassification could change compliance math for SUV-heavy automakers if the rule survives to 2030.
insights.locator: Should these regulations still be in effect

insights.claim: The Obama administration's 2012 CAFE standards targeted 54 mpg by 2025, which the first Trump administration cut in 2020 from 46.7 mpg to 40.4 mpg for model year 2026.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Shows policy whiplash that complicates automaker long-term product planning.
insights.locator: We could have had a better world

insights.claim: The rollback comes just as US fuel prices are climbing higher than Americans have seen before.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Weaker efficiency standards amid record fuel prices increase household energy cost exposure.
insights.quote: Now, it seems we go backward just as fuel prices are climbing higher than Americans have seen before.

insights.claim: The Zero Emissions Transportation Association warns that lowering standards will raise costs for families and risks the global auto market leaving American industry behind.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: US automakers may lose competitiveness in global EV markets.
insights.quote: lowering the bar for innovation risks a future where the global auto market leaves American industry behind
